video_title: Trump CAN’T Fix This | Richard Wolff on Victor Davis Hanson, Iran, and America’s Dying Breath
gist: Economist Richard Wolff argues that Trump is presiding over irreversible US imperial decline, citing failed tariffs, no reshoring, Iran closing the Strait of Hormuz and a fracturing Republican base, and that China is leading a global-south, anti-colonial realignment. He also critiques Victor Davis Hanson's Cold War-era case against socialism, says money in politics undid the New Deal, and proposes worker co-ops (via his organization Democracy at Work) as the structural fix.

insights.claim: Wolff argues the best of the American empire is behind it, that Trump (like Biden before him and whoever follows) is presiding over a structural decline, and that the US political class of both parties denies it.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Frames US policy volatility as decline management rather than a cyclical setback; expect continued over-promising by incumbents.
insights.quote: the best of the American empire is behind it. I know that's not fashionable.

insights.claim: Wolff uses an Alcoholics Anonymous framework: the US cannot address its problems until its leaders publicly admit the decline, and he sees that consciousness emerging only slowly.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Political rhetoric promising restoration ('Make America Great Again') is a symptom of denial, which he expects to persist.
insights.quote: we have to get out of an addiction to the nonsense that we are what we aren't anymore.

insights.claim: Wolff claims that in the US two-party system the incumbent is structurally unable to deliver on promises, so power alternates between Republicans and Democrats who differ only on secondary issues, not basic economics or foreign policy.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Expect policy continuity on core economics and foreign policy regardless of which party wins.
insights.quote: It is built in the party in power cannot do what it promises thereby leaving the field to the party that's out of power

insights.claim: Wolff contrasts Germany's large central-Berlin museum confronting the Nazi era with the absence of any comparable US institution on slavery or Native American genocide, and says the Trump administration worked to purge the Smithsonian's historical engagement, including removing its Black director.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Cultural-institution politics is part of the same denial dynamic he sees in economic policy.
insights.quote: Nothing like that exists in the United States. Nothing.

insights.claim: Wolff says previous presidents took visiting leaders like Khrushchev to Detroit auto plants to show off a unionized, integrated working class, but Trump cannot because Detroit's population fell from 2 million in 1970 to 700,000 today, so instead he showed Xi Jinping the renovated White House.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Deindustrialization has removed the showcase of broadly shared prosperity from US soft power.
insights.quote: in 1970 the population of Detroit was 2 million. Today it's 700,000.

insights.claim: Wolff describes the US as the world's biggest debtor country, with China as the number-two creditor of the United States.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: He sees the debt relationship with the main strategic rival as a weakness.
insights.quote: United States the biggest debtor country in the world and China is the number two creditor of the United States in the world.

insights.claim: Wolff argues that in every declining empire the rich and powerful shift the costs of decline onto the middle and bottom, citing Vance boasting of removing 750,000 families from Obamacare and Musk's DOGE chainsaw job cuts.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Predicts continued cuts to social programs and public jobs while elite wealth is protected.
insights.quote: they offload the costs of decline onto the middle and the bottom.

insights.claim: Wolff says Trump has 'far exceeded' his expectations for self-destruction and hopes Republicans vote in November 2026 as if Trump is on the ballot, producing a hostile House and/or Senate.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: He expects disillusioned Republicans to swing the midterms against Trump, constraining his agenda.
insights.quote: Mr. Trump has far exceeded my expectations in the extent of his self-destruction.

insights.claim: Wolff claims Trump failed on his core promises: he did not end the Gaza horror or the Ukraine war, and instead added a war with Iran, which a friend of Wolff's called an 'immense nothing burger'.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: The gap between promises and results is what Wolff thinks erodes Trump's base.
insights.quote: he delivered an immense nothing burger.

insights.claim: Wolff argues tariff threats only work for a country that actually runs the world; once US hegemony has faded, blanket tariffs become absurd, which is why even a Trump-friendly Supreme Court would not uphold them.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Tariffs signal weakness rather than leverage once the US can no longer enforce them.
insights.quote: But when you do it and you can't, which is where we are, it becomes ridiculous.

insights.claim: Wolff argues Trump's tariffs themselves block reshoring, since no rational investor builds a factory in a country where erratic tariffs used as a cudgel could raise input costs, so the manufacturing jobs lost from 1970 to 2010 will not come back.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Tariff unpredictability deters FDI into US manufacturing, beyond a handful of photo-op reshorings.
insights.quote: No one in their right mind would move their factory to the United States.

insights.claim: Wolff says that because Trump cannot deliver the manufacturing jobs that disappeared, he will lose the voters who elected him for that promise.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Shrinking working-class support is a political risk for Republicans.

insights.claim: Wolff claims Trump attacked Iran and Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, which had been open for 50 years, and the US could not reopen it in two attempts (June last year and again since February), with or without a blockade.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Wolff frames the Hormuz closure as a lasting strategic defeat, which matters for oil and shipping risk.
insights.quote: The straight of Hormuz was open. It's been open for 50 years. He attacks Iran and they close it. And he can't do anything.

insights.claim: Wolff says Trump openly treats the presidency as a way to make money, recalling Trump saying before taking office that if he couldn't make it pay, something was wrong with him.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Expect conflicts of interest and personal enrichment to stay a political liability.
insights.quote: if I can't make this a paying proposition for me, then there's something wrong with me.

insights.claim: Wolff says a significant part of Trump's base is turning on him, with figures like Tucker Carlson and Marjorie Taylor Greene attacking him and serious efforts to invoke the 25th Amendment, which consolidates a majority against him while hardening a roughly 30% core.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: A fracturing coalition but a locked-in core of about 30% suggests a polarized, sticky floor of support.
insights.quote: There's almost another one every day or every few days.

insights.claim: Wolff explains loyalty among Trump's remaining supporters as con-victim psychology: people stay with the swindler rather than admit they were gullible.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Core support may be less sensitive to bad outcomes than polling on policy would suggest.
insights.quote: Every flim flam man in the history of flim flam, every crook, every hustler, every swindler has always had that.

insights.claim: Wolff calls Trump's promise of $5,000 per American if Republicans win both chambers vote-buying, possibly criminal, and says most of Trump's past cash promises never materialized.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Treat campaign cash-transfer promises as unlikely to be paid out.
insights.quote: This is an attempt by Mr. Trump to buy votes.

themes.theme: Iran, China and the anti-colonial realignment

insights.claim: Wolff says Iran, with 93 million people, has stymied the United States, and calls this historic because Iran matches US firepower with ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones that it can hide, can use to devastate US allies and can turn on US bases, which Vietnam and Afghanistan never could.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Cheap missile and drone capability narrows the US military edge and puts regional bases and allies at risk.
insights.quote: we can devastate your allies in and we can lay waste to your military bases. None of that happened before.

insights.claim: Wolff counts US wars as losses: the Communist Party still runs Vietnam, the Taliban runs Afghanistan, and Iraq is closer to Iran than ever.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: History suggests US military interventions do not achieve regime change, so be skeptical of claims that Iran will capitulate.
insights.quote: Who runs Afghanistan today? The Taliban. Another clue.

insights.claim: Wolff frames the present as an anti-colonial era in which the global south, led by China, is redividing an unequal world economy that capitalist imperialism built, enriching Western Europe, North America and Japan.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: He expects the BRICS bloc to become more cohesive and global economic power to keep shifting toward China.
insights.quote: Yes, we're glad you made a world economy, but you did one hell of a bad job, and we're going to fix it now.

insights.claim: Wolff says Iran could not confront the US, and Russia could not confront Europe, without China's backing, making China the anchor of the BRICS and global south bloc.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: China is the key variable behind both the Middle East and Ukraine conflicts.
insights.quote: Iran could not confront the United States if it didn't have the support of China.

insights.claim: Wolff calls China the most remarkable economic development in human history, faster over four decades than Britain, Germany, the US or Japan, and says it now leads the US in trains and electronic payments.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: He thinks Americans underrate China as a competitor and that its development model should be studied.
insights.quote: China is the most incredible [clears throat] experience the human race has so far achieved in the amount of economic development in four decades.

insights.claim: Wolff puts GDP at roughly $4-5 trillion for Russia, comparable to Britain, France or Italy, about $20 trillion for China and $30-35 trillion for the US, arguing that China, unlike the Soviet Union, is a real economic peer and is catching up fast.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Treat China, not Russia, as the US's real economic rival.
insights.quote: The United States 30 35 trillion. China 20 trillion. You understand? China is a real competitor and catching up fast.

insights.claim: Wolff reads Trump's moves (menacing Greenland, talk of retaking the Panama Canal, seizing Maduro, pushing Canada to become the 51st state) as the last gasps of colonialism that show weakness, not strength, and say they pushed Canada toward the EU.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Aggressive US posturing may push allies into other alignments and strengthen rival blocs.
insights.quote: These are the lame, desperate, last gasps of a colonialism that doesn't want to recognize itself for what it is.

insights.claim: Wolff says US missile strikes on small boats in the Caribbean have killed over 200, possibly 250, people over six months with no trial, even though drug dealing is not a capital crime in the US.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: He sees escalating extrajudicial force as a sign of weakness covered over with bravado.
insights.quote: No trial, no lawyer, no jury, no confronting evidence, summary execution without anything.

insights.claim: Wolff argues Europe backs the Ukraine war because its colonial wealth is gone and it hopes that defeating Russia would let it carve up the largest country on earth; he adds that NATO broke promises not to expand east, as Angela Merkel and others have admitted.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: He reads European war spending as economically self-destructive and unpopular with ordinary Europeans.
insights.quote: Europe knows that its wealth is ebbing away. It has been for a century. The European countries are in a mad rush to become tourist attractions.

insights.claim: Wolff argues Israel is less secure than ever after heavy damage from Iranian missiles, drones and Hezbollah, and because US public opinion has swung from pro-Israel to pro-Palestinian over the last two years despite AIPAC spending.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: The midterms could bring in more members of Congress who are skeptical of Israel, putting future US support at risk.
insights.quote: public opinion over the last two years has shifted from being pretty seriously pro- Israel to being pretty seriously pro Palestinian.

themes.theme: Socialism's US revival vs Cold War thinking

insights.claim: Wolff says socialism is surging in the US, with socialists winning office (the mayor of New York and congresswomen in Colorado and Florida), which put Victor Davis Hanson on the back foot in their Piers Morgan debate.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Democratic-socialist candidates are a growing electoral force, not a fringe.
insights.quote: Socialists are running for office. Socialists are winning office.

insights.claim: Wolff argues that Cold War persecution froze American understanding of socialism around 1945, so critics like Hanson recite arguments 70 years out of date and miss post-Soviet developments in Marxist theory and China's rise.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Explains why US elites misjudge both domestic socialist momentum and China.
insights.quote: he's rehashing an argument he's 70 years out of date

insights.claim: Wolff says Hanson repeated a claim that Ilhan Omar is worth $30 million, while her disclosures show joint couple assets of $18,000-$65,000 and her husband's two small companies are worth under $1 million combined.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Wolff uses it to show that the 'socialists are rich elites' argument rests on false figures.
insights.quote: Two joint assets as a couple uh range between $18,000 and $65,000

insights.claim: Wolff sees lingering Cold War trauma in his students aged 20 to 35: they support activist causes such as cutting tuition but will not attend demonstrations because of a vague, inherited fear of political involvement.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Mobilization on the US left may trail its stated support for some time.

insights.claim: Wolff says the minimum wage was last raised in 2009, to $7.25 an hour, and neither Biden nor Trump raised it over the 17 years since, despite rising prices.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Real wages for the lowest-paid have eroded for years, a sign of how far New Deal gains have been reversed.
insights.quote: When was the last time the minimum wage was raised in the United States? Answer. 2009.

insights.claim: Wolff warns that Mamdani-style socialism (free buses, rent freezes, city groceries paid for by taxing the rich) will be undone, as the New Deal was after 1945, unless profits are taken out of corporate hands.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Without structural change, redistribution programs are likely to be reversed over time.
insights.quote: You can't leave the profits in the hands of the corporations.

insights.claim: Wolff says the New Deal was effectively socialist and happened only because two socialist parties, a communist party and the CIO union drive pushed Roosevelt from below; he sees DSA trying to repeat that with a Democratic administration.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Pressure from below, not individual politicians, drives major policy change.

themes.theme: Money in politics and candidate capture

insights.claim: Wolff argues that under universal suffrage the rich must neutralize the majority by buying politicians, so getting money out of politics is the first socialist priority.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Campaign-finance structure determines whether majorities can tax concentrated wealth.
insights.quote: They have to neutralize the democracy of the electorate.

insights.claim: Wolff says Michael Bloomberg was the largest single donor against Zohran Mamdani, funding Andrew Cuomo, and that Mamdani won by organizing tens of thousands of door-to-door volunteers to offset the money.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Organized volunteers can beat billionaire money, which is a template for insurgent candidates.
insights.quote: the biggest single donation against Zoron Mandani came from Michael Bloomberg

insights.claim: Wolff says Elon Musk has given hundreds of millions to Trump, funds Ken Paxton against Talarico in Texas and backs Reform in the UK, calling him on his way to becoming the first trillionaire.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: A single billionaire's cross-border political spending is a growing force in elections.
insights.quote: He's on his way to be the first trillionaire so he can afford to buy parties and candidates in multiple countries

insights.claim: Wolff describes how candidates are sponsored: an economic interest adopts a rising politician through agreements that work like NDAs, which he says explains Vance (Peter Thiel), Rubio (a Florida used-car dealership) and Joe Lieberman (Yale), and party committees screen candidates mainly on how much money they can raise.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Follow the backers to predict a politician's positions.
insights.quote: We're going to support you, but you need to be a reliable spokesman for our interests.

insights.claim: Wolff describes the military-industrial complex and a 'medical industrial complex' (doctors, hospitals, insurers, drug and device makers) as self-reinforcing loops of lobbying money and policy, a model he says Israel's aid-to-donations cycle copies.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Defense and healthcare spending are locked in by political feedback loops, which favors incumbent firms.

insights.claim: Wolff says Yale, tax-exempt with a $25 billion endowment and a $1-1.5 billion budget against New Haven's roughly $300 million, was subsidized by one of the poorest US cities; his 1987 Green Party campaign for alderman to tax Yale won the Republican Party's endorsement.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Tax exemptions for elite nonprofits shift costs onto poor host cities.
insights.quote: Robin Hood in reverse. You steal from the poor to make the rich even richer.

insights.claim: Wolff supports James Talarico and Abdul El-Sayed as better than the alternatives, but worries that because they do not identify as socialists and lack mass organizations behind them, they will win elections without the power to deliver.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Even if progressives win in 2026, Wolff doubts it will produce structural policy change.
insights.quote: You've got to build a movement. That's what you've got to do.

insights.claim: Wolff cites the European model, such as French Socialist Party neighborhood sections that collect monthly dues and can require members to bring up to four people to demonstrations, as the dense organizing US socialists lack; he notes Germany has three socialist parties.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Mass-membership organizing is what Wolff sees as the precondition for lasting left power in the US.

insights.claim: Wolff singles out Republican Thomas Massie as courageous for his Epstein testimony and notes Trump went after him and defeated him in his district.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Trump still controls Republican primaries even while his overall standing weakens.

insights.claim: Wolff proposes worker co-ops as the structural fix, noting that retiring owners of small and mid-sized firms increasingly sell to employees, that Corbyn planned zero-interest loans for co-op buyouts, and that Emilia-Romagna is 40% worker co-ops.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Employee-ownership conversions are a succession route for baby-boomer business owners.
insights.quote: it already has 40% of that area of Italy is worker co-ops.

insights.claim: Wolff says 10% of the richest Americans own 80% of stocks, and that this concentrated owner class used profits to buy politicians who dismantled the New Deal.
insights.speaker: Richard Wolff
insights.so_what: Concentrated equity ownership ties the gains from market returns to political power.
insights.quote: 10% of the richest Americans own 80% of the stocks.
